blocks.x: He couldn't join the sports services and he couldn't make the grades. And he's a piano player.
And trombone ball.
Right, now he decided he's a player and I came back here.
Wait, maybe he'd rather get that on the tape. No, that's okay, go ahead. We've got this second reel on, so it's okay.
I came back here and I have, as usual, two, three jobs. One of them was with Whirline repair department. I took Charlie and repair department. And what were we talking about?
We're talking about Paul Whiteman and Roy Maxwell.

Oh yeah, Paul Whiteman. Well, Paul was playing in New Orleans that week that I'm talking about. And who do I see with the uniform on with Roy Maxwell? I said, man, what you do with that thing on? He said, I'm with Paul. I said, you're with Paul? He said, you have the back. Because he couldn't even read a note when we were at the service and everything. He just played like a spire. And when he said, well, I'll tell you. I said, well, how did you manage to do that? He said, well, I'll tell you what I did, girl. He said, I bought everything that I could find pertaining to a trumpet. And he said, I rented a room outside of New York, way outside. But I wouldn't bother nobody. And he said, I went to work. He said, yeah, I am. Boy, he was there. He felt like a sweet trumpet. Paul put him right away quick. Paul asked me if I let him have him, you see. He was a degree of two months for us to play with. Yeah. Yeah. But, uh. Paul, Paul. Yeah.
That air conditioner makes so much noise. Yeah, it does. Makes it hard for me to hear.

Well, anyhow, he said, that's what I did, girl. And he said, yeah, boy, I wasn't going to go see that. I wasn't going to go hear you, but you'll be a piece. You'll be a piece. You'll be a piece. I want to see some of that stronghold. Yeah. Mm-hmm. So, well, what did you do? Everything they say.
Well, I heard of him somewhere.
He, he, he went right in and took the job as vice chairman for Paul Whiteman. He took the job and he kept it. Mm-hmm.
Yeah, well, that name is very familiar. That's all right. You were at Tom's Roadhouse. So, we got off of that, really, when we got to talking about Tom's Roadhouse.

Well, Tom's Roadhouse is the way I got the job, the first job I got after the service, you know, when I came back from the service. Well, then I went there and, well, a couple of fellas saw me and asked me, I told him, so, so, and so, you know what I mean? Just nothing. I just got in town, come on, play with us and things like that. You know, that's how, that's how it goes. That's how it went, rather, in those days.
You don't remember the guys at Tom's Roadhouse, or do you?
Same guys. They played everywhere. They might be here today and over there tomorrow and over there the next day.
Different guys just walked around while hunting those guys.

No, they're different guys. Same fellas play all the time. Pretty much. Pretty much always. No regular bag. But there's no regular in the all. There's no such thing as hiring by contracts and all that stuff. Yeah. They do that. We just went and played the job. That's all.
Never know when you're going to get fired either, I guess.
No, you never know, but you ought to know if you don't. It's bad because, yeah, we might allow you to get fired.
Well, you can see for yourself. You can see when the people don't like you.
Oh, yes. You don't have to have anybody tell you anything about it. You know.
Well, how long did you stay at Tom's? Very long?

Oh, I don't know. A couple of weeks or so, you know. I don't know. I guess I was born two or three weeks. And then what did you do? Then went to another job somewhere else. Then that was just part of time. They got people like going for Marsden before. No, that was before Marsden. Before Marsden was much later. 28? Yeah.
No, from that. Yeah, the New Orleans jet.
You got this bunch together. Yeah. Oh.

New Orleans jazz babies, huh? Uh-huh. This is marked 1919, the New Orleans jazz babies. Yeah. And it says, Henry Bruni's trombone, Mary Bruni's trumpet. And yourself, of course, I don't know. Sax and clarinet. When did you take up sax, anyhow?
Well, as soon as sax came on the market. See, in those days, they didn't have sax. They didn't have the system in sax.
Did you play sax before you went in the Army?
Uh, well, oh yeah, but you see, uh, your sax and your Army, there's a good space in between there. Good space there.
No, did you play sax in New York?
Yeah, I played, no, no, no, no, not New York, no.
It was after you came back down here.
All I played there was the old Alba system clarinet. Yeah. Nothing else.
I guess they were using the Alba system in those times, just about everybody.

Yeah, there's two instruments that they tried to go with the B flats of sax, you know. Mm-hmm. The, uh, trumpet, really, the trumpet sax. They, uh, put that on the market, you know. Mm-hmm. And so forth. I stuck right to the...
Well, anyway, uh, you took up the sax after you got out the Army, or during... Oh, yeah, after. After the Army.
Oh, yeah, I went all through the Army with the clarinet. With the old, uh, uh, what do you call it again? Albert system.
Albert. So you must have taken up sax about 1918, 1919, you know, when you were with the jazz ladies at small. Yeah. 1919. Must have been one of the very first ones down here to play sax.

Well, we was. I don't know. The only one fellow that I know, and that's the same fellow that I said about playing Napson that I couldn't recall. I got a picture of him in my mind, but I can't call his name. But he had one of those straight, uh, B-flat, you know, the sax. Soprano. Soprano sax, that's right. Yeah. And, uh, I saw the thing and I saw advantages in it because I could do things with it that I couldn't do with the clarinet. Uh-huh. So I got one of the clarinet and sax, saxophone rather.
Did you get an alto or a tenor or a baritone or bass or soprano first? B-flat, soprano.

You got soprano first? Yeah, I started, I started and stayed with the soprano for a long time. I guess I played the soprano over a year before I finally switched over to the alto. And I was on, I stayed on the alto. Uh-huh. Well, tell me a little bit about these, these men and the, uh, five New Orleans jazz babies.

Didn't you say Cassard was in here? Jules? Yes, that's the first one on the line. And what did he play at that time? He played piano. Yeah, well, I've heard him play bass, but I've never heard it on the record.
Well, bass was his, bass was his, uh, real instrument, you see. But he played lots of jazz.
I was on the alto. I was on the alto.
I was on the alto. Uh-huh.
Well, tell me a little bit about these, these men and the, uh, five New Orleans jazz babies. Didn't you say Cassard was in here? Jules?

Yeah, bass was his, bass was his, uh, real instrument, you see. But he played lots of times. He played, uh, sax with us too. You know, they changed it around. It's hard to, it's hard to explain about these jazz men, because they, uh, they, uh, for them, uh, let's see, you want an explanation on them?
Yeah, well, I want to know about him, how he changed around.
Oh, well, he just, like Roy Maxson did.
He could play piano?
Yeah. Play, tum, tum, tum, tum, you know, a compliment.
Chord, yeah.
And that's all, all of them. That's a good chord band was better than, uh, uh, when he's fast from it, you know.
Yeah, you don't want a butterfly piano on a jazz band.
No, indeed. No? No lily bells. You want that harmony to come, too. Yeah. Rhythm. Rhythm, harmony, that's, that's all jazz is, nothing else.
Did you ever know a drummer named Joe H. Try?
I think I very well did. Very, very personal friend of mine.
Who did he play with?
Everybody, anybody. I don't know if George ever played with anybody straight, I mean, as a team, you know. I don't remember if I ever seen him do that.
Well, who was your drummer with the jazz babies?
I'm a boy. Harry Burke?
Mm-hmm. These guys here? Yeah. With the British boys and you.

Yeah, with the Jules and then, uh, there's, uh, there's, uh, uh, uh, Merrick. And me, there's what's going on with this one. Who's this one? Huh? Who's this one? Huh? This is, uh, uh, uh, three, three, three, three, three, five, the trumpet, uh, Henry Brunson. That was Henry Brunson? Yeah. Yeah. And where's Abbie out there? Abbie? Well, Abbie wasn't in this band.
Abbie played trumpet.
He wasn't in that band. He was in the band of the Rice or whatever. He was in the band where?
In the Boxing. No, Abbie, where was he?
Where? Oh, I thought you, in this picture, Abbie's not in there, huh?

No, you asked me about each individual one played in that band. I just wanted to do the drum roll. Well, maybe it was saying one of these pictures. You, you'll run against it if you get enough of that stuff there. You'll find it on Pete Lehmann's, Pete Lehmann's the officer. It's the same man.

Yeah.
Yeah.

Well, I mean...
Trae or his French, he didn't get into French. Yeah. I see.
George Traehan. I don't know if you were going to play with him.
Yeah. I see. George Traehan, I think he's talking about it. I don't know if I say it first. Yeah. Well, where did these New Orleans Jazz Babies play at? You and the Brunies boys?

Where did we play? Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. Pretty much any place in New Orleans is worth playing in. New Orleans? Yeah. I know we... Once the festival was to open the Silver Slipper and the Nut Club and the Lalloo and all these places here in Canada. Yep. And then...

I mean, Bain's system in this picture. 1919. You changed to Bain's system by then. I changed the clarinet. Yeah, Bain's system clarinet. It shows you. See if I can see. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

I said, Big O, I don't want to play that kind of thing. I said, it's nice. I appreciate all that, but I don't want to play. But that's how we got to acquire that. He told me, he said, get your volume system playing. I'll let you play a whole lot more than you are now. And that's how I come in and get a volume system.
Did you execute more than that? No, I didn't. You could play more than that.
Oh, yes, you have. Lots and lots of more bands.

Just popular stuff.

Pop or something. And then the stuff that we make up ourselves. The numbers that we make up. You may come in tonight. Let's see this. You know. And if you're going to play it good, we accept that.
What about angry? You're going to tell me about that if you want to.

That's my number. Yeah, that's my number. I'll say this. The way that... We can restrict it. No, no, I was talking. We were talking. Oh. Oh. That gave me an idea what it is. Angry. Now don't be angry. Cause we'll fight from you all in. Your land and my land. Oh, I forgot the song. Your land and my land. The five babies jazz band. Full of pep. Watch your step grow slower. Now when you hear that trombone play. You think it's simply grand. But the man that's on the library's, he's a melody man. Angry. Now don't be angry. Cause we'll fight from you all in. That was my number. That's what I was talking about. Yeah. That was my number. That's what I was talking about. Yeah. That was my number. That's what I was talking about. Yeah. That was my number. That was my number. So did you play much around New Orleans and other places too?
Did you travel out from the city? With that band? With that band? Yeah, sure we traveled with that band. Where did you go?
Oh, we'd like to take a crazy ocean, work a circle all around, come in by Pensacola, by Mobile and ride on in town and play everything in between.
Well, I know Merritt is over there in Biloxi now. Merritt has been in Biloxi for years.
Since about that time off and on I think. Yeah.

But that nigga could sing good too, yeah. That's very close.

Yes, indeed. I guess so.
He's out in California.
He's been out there for quite a few years.
Yeah, he's been out there.

Now we had another thing that you won't find very often. We had a piano player. We call him Blind Jack. He's blind. Jack, he didn't play with a steady, but pick him up on jobs every night and things like that. Spot jobs. He's the only man that's ever been known to do it when he's going to tell you. He'd leave his home. You tell him, it would be so-and-so, number so-and-so, how so-and-so. And meet up at 8 o'clock, Jack, all right, all right. He's the only man that's ever been known. He can go out to, he can go out to Canaro Street and get on any car he wanted to get on, and nobody helped him at no time. He'd get off at a car when he wanted to get off, and he'd get off at all. He was a beautiful guy. He'd get off at all. That's great.
Some guys just have that. I guess it's an instinct or something. Yeah. Anyway, what kind of jobs did y'all play at that band? Did you play steady dance work?
Yeah, the biggest majority of it was all dance work.
Did you advertise much?
No, I didn't advertise at all. I let the band advertise. Well, that's what I mean.
Did you play advertising jobs on trucks or wagons or? Oh, yes.
I got all kinds. I would parade on the... You paraded, huh? Oh, yes. I paraded. I played all kinds of jobs. So you got around.

Did you ever play any prize fights? No. Never played prize fights. I heard guys talk about that, like Johnny Law and Tony Sparbo and different guys talk about going and playing prize fights between the rounds. Yeah. But I never saw that.
No, I never threw around with that at all.
You didn't like boxing much?

Yes, I liked it so much that I wanted to do it myself. Oh, you wanted to do it? Yes, sir. I started out there and I had pretty good teachers and so forth. The old man told me one day, he says, he said, I'm on a table and eat and he says, how do you like boxing? I just come in. I said, I like it all right, here I'm boxing. He says, I'm going to tell you. He says, you got there and learn all you can learn for self-defense. But today you have to accept the nickel fight. He said, I'm going to get off. He would not let me get in and save his life.
I guess he was afraid you might get punchy or something. Fighting too much, too tough a game.
No, the only way he was peculiar about that fight, didn't he? He was very peculiar about that. That was good self-defense. Learn all you can.
Let's see, I was going to ask you some more about the, what happened after you left the five New Orleans jazz babies? The ringside orchestra. Yeah.

The ringside orchestra. Yeah. The ringside orchestra. The ringside orchestra. Yeah. The ringside straight out. I see the picture. Yeah. It looks like a wrong day. Yeah, this is 1922 to 1923, the ringside.
Yeah, that was Pete Hunland's place.
You know Pete, you know of him.
Yeah, I know. I've seen him, I don't know him.

Pete opened the ringside. Yeah, he opened the ringside and that was considered the best place anywhere around the all this to go to. We had a wonderful, let's see, I put a couple extra men in there. I reckon with jazz bands there were only five men.
Oh yeah? I can see you guys, seven here.
There's Harry Boykin there, we saw him, what, he played on the piano right there? I mean on the drums.
On the drums, yeah. Was Pete Herman blind there?
Oh yeah, blind in his back.
He stopped fighting and all that.
He fought plenty fights blind.

Yeah, I know that, he still goes to them. He sees there in the front row every time there's a fight here in town. He never misses one. Oh Pete. Oh, he's amazing. You've got Oscar Markwood says here on the fiddle. Yeah, that's a fiddle.
That's a jazz fiddle. That's not no regular fiddle, no straight fiddle, that's a jazz fiddle.
I know, I heard him.
You did?
Oh yeah, I knew him. Well he ought to tell you he knew me too. Yeah, well.
Oscar and I don't know, no friends.
He told me he's from across the river and he knew a guy named Emmett Hardy over there. Emmett Hardy, sure. Did you know Emmett? Oh yeah.
He knew Emmett when he was trying to learn how to make a note on the horn.
Oh. Was he good? He developed pretty good.

I don't know, you see I was running all around the country and I understood that he did pretty good. I'll tell you another fellow I started off here was Slovakovich. Oh, thank you, Vodakovich, yeah. I started, I was playing at Tom's Roll-Off. Tom Roll-Off's coming in pretty often the other night even. I was playing at, and Max Fink was a fiddler and so forth. And he asked me one day, he says, girl, if I bring my horn, I bought a horn, if I bring it, he said, would he help me out? I said, sure. Why not? Sure enough, he did. He brought his heart and he sat in there listening, you know, he wasn't making out like he was playing. He wasn't playing. And then Vicky got his thought, that was me.
I guess you helped quite a few of them, did you know?
I helped, I helped quite a few of them.
You know Sharky?
Yeah, I know Sharky very well. I know Sharky, but Sharky wasn't Sharky.
You were just a kid, huh? Just a kid.
So was Vicky. But there's kids, it's about around 17, 16, 17.
Did Sharky play there? No.

I took Sharky right over here at Blutsey, I played a week's engagement there. I took him over there. And he couldn't play on three home. He couldn't play much. I told him to play, keep fighting. I could listen to him, just keep fighting. He did. Years later, I heard that he was doing pretty good.
Oh yeah? He still is, he does alright. He's been out to Texas for a week. To carry Shields and Emil Christian with him.
Sure enough? I was playing with that too. I was one of those pictures. Who? Shields.
You knew the Shields boys?
Yeah, there's a Shields boy. Who was the others? Sharky? The Sharky one of them? No, it was the Shields.
There was Larry and Eddie Shields, and I think one called Pat Shields. I never did know him. I only knew Harry and Larry.
One other fellow I want to tell you about. He was doing good trumpet player too. I've been trying to rake my mind's faith. He was a butcher by trade. Johnny Lawler.
That's correct.
Yeah. I've been trying to say that name for the last 15 minutes.
Yeah.
The old Johnny, old Johnny Lawler.
I haven't seen him for about a year or two.
Oh no, I haven't seen him in 40 years.
Yeah. Still around. He plays piano or something.

Yeah. He plays good accompaniment. Mm-hmm. He plays good accompaniment. What were the most bands you had with the Butcher Brothers from Lafayette? Who were they? Uh, I feel like thinking of names. Warren? No, that's my thoughts. Warren, Warren, I thought. Uh, big old long legged or something. I can't think of him. What did he play? He played drums with us. Well it wasn't very long after the war was over. It was after Pete Herman.
Yeah it was after Pete Herman you went up there? The Stand It All band?
Yeah I'm talking about dates you know. It's hard to remember dates.

Well don't worry about it we got it down on the pictures. What was that Stand It All band like? Did you fit in there okay? Oh yeah. You didn't have any trouble? It must have been a big band huh? You didn't have to read?

Oakland You don't have to move your fingers or anything. While you're at it, why don't you put it in there? Well, there's another number here. I believe I lost track. That's a rooster. Make it different, the old rooster, the young rooster, any way you want it. Well, try it. We'd like to hear it. Give you the whole family rooster.
Oh, yeah.
That's very good.
You can still play the devil out of that thing, I know. I don't see how I'm doing it, though.
That's what I am. You just need some good rhythm underneath you and you can really go to town.
Well, I can play a whore.
He wants a saxophone out here.
I just love a saxophone.
Well, let's see. Did you play full time with that Stand It All band? Oh, yeah. I was employed in the band that imported me there. Old man Webber heard me playing clarinet.
And he had me imported into the plant, you see. And you played every day there? No, no, no. No, no. Just… You were a still worker.
I was working on stills. I was an assistant stillman when I left there. Mm-hmm. Well, I guess those were good times to be working on a still. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Well, I guess those were good times to be working on a still. In those days, you needed a still.
Well, all I had to do was I could go block away if I wanted to sit down and wash it. As long as it didn't blow up, it's all right.
Oh, I see. But y'all weren't making any moonshine. I think that's still just all stuff. He was pushing back to homebrew and forth in those days.

I'm homebrew, though. I made about two glasses. You and that bro made a batch. Me and that bro made us one batch and we put it in the chicken house. Oh, I let them bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop. Went out there in the back quick. My whole brew was popping off one after the other. You made one batch and put it in the stove and put it in the oil wire and put it in the stove. It didn't like it. I'm trying it all right. You didn't have to play all the time. You would watch or steal it? No, we played mostly for just special games. You know what I mean?
Parades? I was saying, you played parades with that band? Mm-hmm.
Well, I played anything they wanted, but all heavy stuff, big heavy stuff. The orchestra, we played jazz music. With the whole band, we played nothing special, but gauges.
You played for dances with that big band ever? No, no, no.
No, I mean special gauges, but I mean like Mardi Gras and all this stuff like that. That's kind of stuff. We played a whole lot of concerts. We did a whole lot of concerts.
Well, where did you go after you left Baton Rouge?

Yeah, I don't know if I'm old. I'm thinking a little. You came back to the Orioles. I know it was back from Young, but just left. You came back to the Orioles and then you went down to Florida Town. Yeah, Florida. And Mobile. That's right. That's where I went back. I used to play that circus from Mobile to Pensacola and all around making the circus.
Well, what would your special derby orchestra be?
There was jazz band. There was jazz band.
There was jazz band. There was jazz band. Tell me a little bit more about it. I see you got some men in here. You got all kind of instruments.
Yeah.
In the pictures.

Well, that little orchestra there I believe had more. I know mine. I've never played any orchestra and had as many pieces as that thing. We had a lot of music. How many men I got? Eight men I believe in it.

Yeah, it's eight men in this picture. And I can see two cornets, a banjo, two fiddles, drums, alto, tenor, soprano. Two paronets, one's an outlet system and one's a bane system. And a tuba in here. No trombone, huh?
No, I believe we took two fiddles instead of the trombone. We took an extra fiddle. Yeah.
And it says on the back, the XANA director, Tuva Gerard Levison, is that his name? Who?
Levy. Oh, Levy? Leviton. Leviton, that's right.
Gerard Levison. Other members, Debbie P. Finkel. Who is Debbie P. Finkel?
Little Finkel. What did he put in here? I know him very well. I was trying to keep an instant take him.
But I think we got it all in here somewhere, aren't we?
Yeah. Remember the battery, not Mitchell? Probably.
Well, Joe Mitchell? Remember him? Yeah. Who is he?

I'll have to look at the van. Mm-hmm. Well, you don't have the instruments there, you know. No. No. Shane Martin. Is that Shane Martin? No, Shane Martin. Shane. I think, uh... I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
So they got Joe Mitchell, Bob Robinson, Victor Corsi.
I think that's Joe Mitchell, if I'm not mistaken. He played Gana. And he also played Sticks. Marimba. Marimba. Marimba.
Bob Robinson, Joe Waddle, and Edward J. Powers, the sax wizard.
Yep.
Yep.
Yeah. You know, you get his horn. See, the horn, I mean, it's really right. Yeah. Well, what... Ed Powers was a guest. Yeah. He was a guest. I see.
And he... What's... You said you were playing the soprano and alto, so... Yeah. What instrument did he play?
Ed Powers played the tenor.
Mm-hmm.
I played the alto and the soprano, and Ed Powers played the tenor.

I guess he must have been playing the Albert system. He was. Yeah. Because it shows in the picture, one Albert and one Bane system. Well, anyway, where did y'all play? I see in the Scrab Bucket's got the Ratskeller there. What was that?
That Ratskeller, that was Pensacola Ratskeller or Mobile? Oh, it doesn't say.
Mobile? Mobile.
Right across from the...what do you call them? The Battle House? In the Battle House Hotel.
Yeah.
In there. Oh.
I see. Right in the Battle House Hotel. Yeah. On the bottom floor. That was a restaurant-like or just a drink?

Well, they would rope that off, you see, the section where they're dancing and so forth would be. They'd rope that off. And ordinarily, we'd just play on concert music, you know. You'd call it concert if you want. It's not a high-class concert. It's what we call concert. Dinner music. Yeah, just dinner music. Dinner music.
Play quiet, huh?
That's right, yeah.
Down low, get soft. Mm-hmm. Did you ever cut loose? Oh, yeah.

Put them in the alley there? Oh, yeah. We cut loose every once in a while. They want that, huh? They can't do that when it's just about time to last while the six and fall asleep. And you wake him up.
Well, what was Florida town?

Florida town is, what is that, outside of bathing and stuff, whatever. It's a summer resort and pavilion. Oh, yeah. It's a small town. It's across. It's across from Blux. It's about 10, 15 miles out of Pensacola.
North of Pensacola. North of Pensacola. Yeah, that's right. And you played there in Florida town, didn't you? Oh, yeah.

Played there. We used to make a regular tour of that. Mobile, Pensacola, Florida town, all of those that come in. The owner who manages me at the familiar Florida town was Burgess Pace, wasn't it? Yeah. The Battle House Mobile was pecked, S.H. Peck. That one would pecked himself. It says something about the dance at the Mary Gardens tonight.
Purple Derby's present Mr. L.E. Clough, New Ideas and Trumpets Information. I never heard of L.E. Clough.
Well, if I'm not mistaken, I think he came from Chicago. I think he's pretty sure. I don't think he was from Chicago. I was a friend and we just took him along and was very hard. I don't know.
Pavilion comfortably heated. Everybody has a good time at Florida town. That must have been in Florida town, the Mary Gardens. Mm-hmm. Wasn't Bill Lagman?
No, the Mary Gardens, the Mary Gardens, that's the bottom floor where he used to rope it off there for dances. I mean, it's the very very, yeah.
And wasn't Bill Lagman from over there in that neighborhood? Ryan Mobile or something? Did you know him? Well, that might have been later.
Yeah, I don't recall anything.
Well, anyway, back to this. Why did they call you the Purple Derbies?
I don't know where I got that.
But you wore Purple Derbies, you said earlier.
Well, yeah, I didn't wear it around the streets when I wore it to work, you know. When you were playing, huh?
Yeah.
It was a lot of fun. Is there anything to make the people talk? Oh, yeah. The more they talk, the more they keep you in mind. Mm-hmm.
Since the Mary Gardens was a hotel and pavilion on beautiful Escambia Bay. Bay. Yeah. And you had to, you played New Year's dances for the, let's see, the Battle House. Yeah. You had to do yesterday.

Yeah. Well, the Battle House is where we used to rope that off. I don't remember whether they changed the name of that particular department or not. We used to play on the bottom floor. And it, it rope the main entrance off. Nobody could get in with the one of those.
Well, it says here, the green room at the Battle House. Green room, that's it.
Yeah.

From now through Mardi Gras. Dancing from 9 PM in the green room at the Battle House every Wednesday and Saturday nights. Table service with a cover charge of a dollar and a half. That would make it some money. CLC script dance every Friday. I guess that was a club. A strip dance?
Script.
Script. Subscription. Well, that's something else.
Oh, it wasn't.
And then it says, Gentleman, a dollar and a half. Music by the Purple Derby office.

You'll see another one in there too. Where they are charging six dollars. That's New Year's. Well, that's a... He had a famous slogan in there along about that time too. All those who can dance, what? What was your slogan? You can't dance, hang on and what? Hang on and ride. Hang on and ride. Hang on and ride. Hang on and ride. Hang on and ride. It said...

Excuse me, go ahead. It's in one of those clubs. Yeah. I'm afraid to handle these. Unless I do a very care. But it says here you play the New Year's dance, New Year's Eve. Start at 11 and end at 6. You kept up some hours in.
They had to hang on, that's all.

And the Bithian Sisters Dance, Entertainment and Dance, Monday night, November the 15th, 1926 at the Elks Club from 8 to 12. Assessment of a dollar and a quarter. Ladies free. And then you played on the radio too.
Yeah.
This is the COA Pensacola, huh?
Uh-huh. What's his name called? Roger's Base. No. Not the radio. No, they had the radio.
Johnny Frankel was the announcer.
That's it. That's correct. Johnny Frankel. I didn't call his name to save my life.
How'd you do on the radio? Did you make any money?

We did. No, we didn't. We just played one engagement there, you see. And that was all good. But we had very good luck with it. Our announcer told me, he said, your wife is beautiful. She's coming fine.
Here's the Ratscull. This is at 107 West Gregory.
Gregory Street. That'd be Mobile.

That's Mobile. That's Grabhouse. And the Merry Gods, you've got again. Chicken Bill is $1. That's expensive. For those days, I guess. They're paying for the music. The Green Room has a New Year's Eve dance beginning at 9 p.m. This must have been a different year. New Year's Night dance beginning at 9 p.m. Scripts. Gentlemen, $2. Fun, Favors, and Frolic. Buffet dance on Wednesday, December the 29th, $2.50. And then New Year's Eve, breakfast and dinner dance, 11 to 6 a.m. $6. That's when you got the $6 on those seven hours.
We didn't have the right price. We said we thought they could pay the pay. That's all.

Oh, yeah. And then here's the Battle House again. The Purple Derby Orchestra has been engaged for the season. It plays at luncheon hours, 12.30 to 2 p.m. So you play lunch, huh? Yeah. And from 6.30 to 8 p.m. at dinner hour, the orchestra will play for the New Year's Eve, celebrate it, fresh in the beginning, 11 p.m. and continue until 6 a.m. and cover charge, $3.00. And then Sanders Beach, you play Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Grand opening, July the 26th, 1927.
That's correct.

Oh, yeah. So you must have done all right. You played the Florida Town Pavilion for the Red Cross Life Saving Group. The Purple Derby Orchestra. That's out of the scrapbook. Yeah. This Red Cross deal, you got a dollar on a koala. Here's another one for the Sanders Beats. Even had free motion pictures. The New Pleasure Palace in Florida Town. No, they played the party town. No, they played the party town. Oh, Pensacola's New Pleasure Palace. You played there. Here's a script dance. The Swift and Company's office for Andalusia. That's Andalusia. That was a dance, it was it?
Yep.

Attend a good script dance. Oh. Music by the Purple Derby Orchestra. That's a good script. That's not until first it won't get it, sir. You were going to tell me about how you might have taught music at Milton High, it says here. That's right. But you didn't do it after all, huh? Mm-hmm.

I don't know, but I'm trying to think in my head why I refuse it after. And you didn't have a high school diploma? I don't know whether it's like that or not. More than like it was, I don't know the course. Did you ever teach anybody? Oh, yeah.
I've never finished anybody.
I'd give them a start, that's all.
How'd you start them off? By a year, just quickly?
No. Regular, regular booking, you know? Method line? Method. I'd take a method and start from the bottom.
And the rule is by the time they get to playing, they got to get them ready to turn them loose. Who did you teach? Do you remember any of them?
Anybody. A lot of them, huh? Mm-hmm. Let's see. Here's one.
Here's one. A Midsummer Ball. Woodman Circle Clubhouse. And the Lugia, Alabama. Friday night, July 22nd, 9 until question mark.
That was a pickup, you see, right between the big jobs.
Oh, yeah.
Making the cycles. He's a player cycle.
Good. You must have done a lot over there. Well, what is this Vasco's of Slidell that you have there? A Saturday Night Treat.
Saturday Night Treat.
A father of jazz with his singing sax in Dixieland. Rock and roll.
That's what he said, Jim.
Yeah.
For your listening and dancing pleasure, that's why you're yawning jazz. Rock and roll.
That must have been late years if it says rock and roll.
That's the rock and roll. And let's see. The last thing it says is rock and roll. Mm-hmm.
And here's dance. Grand opening Saturday, June 9th, Eaton's Club, Henderson Point, Pass, Christian. That would be true.
We have skipped a clutter area there. Yeah. These are late things, huh? Yeah. He skipped quite a while during the compression when he was playing at Morrison's interview. Oh, yeah.
Well, that's... Yeah. Then let me go back a little while to Morrison's end. When did you play at Morrison's?

I was waking to the Whirlands. You know, repair department. I had a charge of repair department. And while I was there, Morrison wanted to go over and play a dinner dance. Well, not dance. I mean, just a dinner concert. Yeah. And he liked it. Mm-hmm. So, we saw... I'd make one at 12, and then I'd go back at 5 and make one. But I played two concerts a day in my repair department. Mm-hmm. And you were also at that time playing a theater version. Yeah, sang a... Sang a theater? I was just replacing... You know, playing a pit. Yeah, playing a pit, but I was just... I was just replacing a little... What's his name again? This was from London, wasn't it? He thought it was a regular show. Playing a pit. It's a regular show.
You know who was just here in town? Huh? About a week was Al Galador. Do you remember him?
No.
I didn't know what he said.
He quit. Al Galador.
He left town in... Galador. He left town in about 35. He played at the Orpheum for a long time. Yeah. With Joe Fulco. Mm-hmm. I thought you might remember him.
No, I don't really know Fulco. Yeah, he and...
He and Boris... Howard Glories were in the band, I think, and... Mike Kaplan. You know Mike Kaplan? Yeah, I don't know Mike Kaplan.
I know him. I don't know him.
Anyway, he played at... At Morrison's. Yeah.
Morrison's Capitol Theater.

Yeah, I saw in a magazine... You remember when the union used to put a little magazine out? The Musicians' Union? Called the Prelude. I doubt if you remember that. But they had it in May of 1928. You were playing in Morrison's. I found that. And then it says you went with Buzzy Williams to the Slipper in October of 28. Yeah. You remember Buzzy? Oh, yeah. He's a night watchman now. Pan American Life Insurance. Last time I saw him, he was out there. I'd like to know, Buzzy. I haven't seen Buzzy Cock in a year. Well, I haven't seen him for a while, but the last I heard of him, he was out there.

Yeah. Just like the other night there, I said, yeah, no, I'm alive about three weeks ago. Mm-hmm. I get a letter in the mail, and I open it. And it's been so long since I've seen the boy, I didn't remember his name. Jake can't tell me who he was. Mm-hmm. And somebody sends me a letter, and greetings, you know, that I let nobody else in my piano play. I used to play with Mr. Griffo. What was his name? Emmett. No. Martin. Joe Martin. Huh? Joe Martin.
Joe Martin.
Huh? This is a recent group.
Oh.
Huh?
Anyway, you remember that band at the Slipper? You remember playing with Buzzy there, huh?
Oh, gosh, yeah. I don't know what he was wearing for years and years. Years. Not one day.
What was the Slipper like then, in those days?
It was a nice little place. It was nothing. A library, but very nice.
I know Abby was in there for a while, Abby Burney's.

Well, yes. Well, that's what I was trying to tell you. Well, go ahead. It's hard to say who's who and why to be accurate with it because of the fact that you get so many jump ins and outs and ins and outs.
How many Morrisons' cafeterias were there in those days? Was there just one or two?
No, there was, I think there was two. I think there was two.
You played in them both or just one?
Yeah, I played in them both.
You played in both, huh?
They had one up in town, you see, and one of them out on the highway. You played the one in town? Yeah, I played for one in town. I can remember that one.
Yeah.
And you were just about getting in remembering size. Not that size. I sat on the back.
Is that the same place as the one that's now? St. Marshall. Still running out of here.
Still running out of here. Still running out of here. Yeah. Still running out of here. Yeah. Oh.

Oh. Well, anyway, did you have much trouble with musicians that would sign up and leave or something? I noticed that there was a resolution made to the union by you. You know, they passed some law that musicians couldn't sign a contract unless they could fulfill it. You don't remember anything about that, huh? That was... Leave? Yeah. Yeah, that was in the union records. You've forgotten it. That was 1928.

Oh, listen, I know what they're talking about. I had a contract for, I believe it was two months or six months or something like that in Shreveport. I wanted to join the union. They told me I had to join the union. I said, okay. I went to sign the papers, you know. Some, they got messing around. Some kind of way got me mad. I told them where they could go and I left. And I went to Shreveport, but they didn't have a job. The job wasn't available.
The job wasn't an entry for? No.
Because he didn't get into the union. I didn't join the union.
Oh, yeah. Well, I didn't need the union.
Why did you spend all that money for the union? Well, that's not what he's talking about. That one. He's asking your mind. Is that at one time you were in the union and you made a resolution?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah. That's a resolution. I don't know what that is.
That musicians shouldn't sign a contract unless they can fulfill it.
Well, that's a deadless fact.
What about, you know Johnny Harmon? Very well. Yeah, he worked at Whirlines, didn't he?
Oh, I don't know.
Maybe not when you were there. Florese was in the Whirlines. Florese?
Florese, he's waking at night. He was, rather.
I think A.J. LaCosta's retired. He doesn't know about Farrell.
There was also that blind man working at Whirlines. Yeah, that old blind guy.
Blind Jack was a man?
He worked as a guy with one of his names. What was that real name? We used to call him Fort Bell.
Well, I'll ask somebody wearing Whirlines. They might remember him.
Yeah, well, I...
And Eddie Benton was there for a while. Eddie Benton, he was a trombone player. Worked at Whirlines before. I didn't know him. A little probably didn't know him.

Will an aide go to room two, please. Room two for an aide, please. I think that just about after Morrison's and the slipper, and the nut club and the Ladoo, that's where he dropped out of music. That's where he dropped out at that time. Long enough to settle down so I could go to school. We were in the ground and we were changing schools. It didn't break, so he stayed together.
About what year was that you might remember?
I think that this was around 1931-32.
The Depression was on then, too. That one's a bit tough.

Well, he played the Morrison's during the Depression. Probably had gone back to Morrison's after these other engagements. He didn't pick up with his music again until these Willis Fall bands came together.
We've got a picture from the Hambone Inn. It says, it's you on saxophone, F.J. Curley-Lazana. And there's a clarinet in the picture, too. That's his. And one of the guitar players is named Bobby.

Yeah, that was Bobby. We showed it to you a long time ago. We didn't get Bobby's last name. We didn't get the other guitar player. Didn't get his last name? Dan Seals, who was the owner of the Hambone Possible. Seals, the owner. He played an officer, too. He was the owner. He was a bass player. Yeah, he played bass and he played guitar, too. Yeah. Dan played bass and guitar. And what's the most?
This is Hambone Inn, 1952. Hansborough, Mississippi. Pass Road.
That's Back Road. They call it Pass Road the old Back Road.

And Bosco's of Slidell must have been about the same time, he says. Right. It was in to Saturday Night 3. And that's the best love club also comes in at the same time. Eaton's Club also comes in about the same time. Dancing on Sundays, 2 to 8 p.m. Music by the Blue Moves. Wow. Yeah, that was another band. Commission, 75 cents. Tell your friends. Thanks, Eaton.
You know why I wasn't there.
The Richard.
G-A-R-R-I-G-A. That's how it was, 65 cents.
What's the name? G-A-R-R-I-G-A. Garriga. Garriga. G-A-R-R-I-G-A. Garriga. I'm not good on these names. But you didn't come back into music until about 1950 and so on. Late years.

Mm-hmm. No, not David was. He was playing Back Bay High School with Mary Brunas, Abby Brunas, who was the other bunch of that band in 19... Jules, I guess. No. That was in 1952. We were playing there in 1952. We were playing together again. The Brunas was.
Oh, yeah.

I remember that. Oh, we used to pull apart and go back together and pull apart. I heard about that. Yeah. We had a dance every Saturday night when we were back in high school. Yeah, but that was the standard gate. Every Saturday night.

When I saw them, they were at Baracell. Do you know where Baracell is? Right on the... It's on the beach, huh? On the beach, yeah. They were there for a while. But they had a different clarinet where they had this Jules Gallo.
Yeah, Jules. Jules Gallo. I don't know if that's why I wanted you up.
Yeah, I think so.
I wasn't going.
Just about got it. I don't want to keep you up too late.
You just stay behind me. It was too late.
Well, we... Yeah, we sure appreciate it, Mr. Luzon.
It's my pleasure giving it to you.
Yeah, well, I've been hearing about you.
If I think if any more, I'll give you some more.

All right. Good. I've been hearing about you for so many years now. It's been, I guess, eight years now I've been hearing about you. Something like that. You know, from the Brunies boys and different people that took up after you, you know, that they admire. A clarinet player from the name of John Handy that told me about you.
John Handy is an old time. I guess John Handy, I don't know if I remember him. He was an old man when I was a young one.
That must be his son.
Well, it could be.
What did John Handy play?
If I can remember right, I think Johnny was a base player.
Might have been. But from up in past, Chris and Jan.
Mm-hmm. Yeah. They were all born in past. I'm pretty sure they were. They were an old relative.
Johnny and Sylvester and you. The young one told me that you helped him out to get started in the barber. That's how I knew it must be you when you said you were a barber.
I've done a little bit of everything and nothing much of a knife.
Well, the tape's running out. And it's almost 10 o'clock. So we better call it to a halt then. So thank you again.
Well, good.
You're making history. Finally got a little credit due to you. Not enough. Well, you can.

segments.chapter: Back from service and early jobs
segments.title: Reel change and return to a repair-department job
segments.summary: A second reel goes on; Lizana says he came back to New Orleans and held two or three jobs, one in a repair department.

segments.chapter: Back from service and early jobs
segments.title: Roy Maxwell, a trumpeter who bluffed his way into Paul Whiteman's band
segments.summary: A service buddy who could not read music taught himself trumpet in a rented room and landed a top job with Paul Whiteman.

segments.chapter: Back from service and early jobs
segments.title: Tom's Roadhouse as first job after service; pickup hiring
segments.summary: First job after the service came from fellows who heard him; no contracts, the same men played everywhere, and he stayed only a couple of weeks.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Taking up soprano sax, then alto, while keeping the Albert clarinet
segments.summary: Asked about a 1919 photo, he explains he played Albert-system clarinet in the Army, then took up soprano sax after seeing one, later alto.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Jules Cassard's versatility on bass, piano and sax; rhythm and harmony
segments.summary: Cassard's real instrument was bass but he played piano and sax too; Lizana says a jazz piano should supply chords, rhythm and harmony.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Who played drums, trumpet and trombone in the Jazz Babies; where they played
segments.summary: Confused photo identification: drummers Harry Burke and George Trehan, Henry and Merritt Brunies, Abbie not in the band; venues like the Silver Slipper and Nut Club.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Switching to Boehm clarinet after pressure from Picou
segments.summary: He changed early from the Albert to the Boehm system after an older clarinetist kept offering to teach him and urged him to switch.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Repertoire of the Jazz Babies and his number 'Angry'
segments.summary: The band played popular tunes and its own numbers; Lizana recites the lyrics of 'Angry' as his number.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Touring from New Orleans to Mobile and Pensacola with the band
segments.summary: The band travelled a circuit along the Gulf coast; Merritt Brunies has long lived in Biloxi.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: 'Angry' as a hit swing number; a street-corner guitar singer
segments.summary: Back-and-forth about how good a number 'Angry' is, then a street singer with a guitar whose name he cannot recall.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Blind Gilbert and the blind pianist Blind Jack
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about blind trumpeter Gilbert; Lizana describes Blind Jack, who took spot jobs and travelled the city alone.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Dance work, advertising and parading jobs
segments.summary: Most of the work was dance jobs; he let the band do the advertising and also played parades and advertising wagons.

segments.chapter: Five New Orleans Jazz Babies
segments.title: Boxing lessons and never playing prize fights
segments.summary: He never played prize fights but loved boxing; a teacher taught him self-defense and would not let him fight professionally.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: The Ringside orchestra at Pete Herman's place, 1922-23
segments.summary: Looking at a 1922-23 photo, Lizana says Pete Herman opened the Ringside, the best place around; the band had added men and Harry Boykin on drums.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: Pete Herman, the blind boxer who never misses a fight
segments.summary: They talk about Pete Herman fighting blind and still attending every local fight.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: Oscar Markwood on jazz fiddle and Emmett Hardy
segments.summary: Oscar is the jazz fiddler in the picture; the interviewer relays that Oscar knew Emmett Hardy from across the river.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: Starting young players: a young horn player, Sharky and the Shields boys
segments.summary: Lizana tells how he helped a youngster who brought a new horn to Tom's, took Sharky along on a week's engagement, and recalls the Shields brothers.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: Johnny Lawler the butcher trumpeter and the Butcher brothers
segments.summary: Lizana finally names trumpeter Johnny Lawler, then tries to recall drummers who ran a butcher business in Lafayette.

segments.chapter: Ringside orchestra and New Orleans players
segments.title: Ringside instrumentation: banjo, jazz violin, saxes and a Chicago pianist
segments.summary: Photo details: Angelo played banjo like a pianist, Oscar played melody on violin, no trumpet, and a Chicago pianist was a fine accompanist.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge big band and New York
segments.title: Moving to Baton Rouge after Pete Herman
segments.summary: He went to Baton Rouge not long after the war and after the Ringside, but cannot pin down dates.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge big band and New York
segments.title: The Standard Oil big band and its photographs
segments.summary: He was hired because of his clarinet and read only when he wanted; the interviewer counts instruments in two big-band photos.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge big band and New York
segments.title: The eight-piece jazz band drawn from the big band
segments.summary: The jazz band had eight pieces who could switch instruments and play anything, such as High Society and Livery Stable Blues.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge big band and New York
segments.title: Livery Stable Blues, the rooster clarinet effect, and vaudeville in New York
segments.summary: He explains who played the rooster part, says they went into vaudeville rather than record in New York, and demonstrates the rooster crow.

segments.chapter: Baton Rouge big band and New York
segments.title: Standard Oil job as assistant stillman, homebrew, and the company band's duties
segments.summary: He was imported to the plant for clarinet, worked on stills, joked about homebrew, and the band played parades, Mardi Gras and concerts.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Leaving Baton Rouge for Mobile, Pensacola and the circus circuit
segments.summary: After Baton Rouge he came back to the Gulf Coast, playing the circuit from Mobile to Pensacola.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Purple Derby Orchestra members and instrumentation
segments.summary: Looking at a photo of the eight-man orchestra, they name members such as Joe Mitchell and Ed Powers on tenor; Lizana played alto and soprano.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Playing dinner music at the Ratskeller in Mobile's Battle House
segments.summary: The orchestra played roped-off dinner music at the Battle House, cutting loose now and then.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Florida Town pavilion and Mary Gardens on Escambia Bay
segments.summary: Florida Town is a summer resort outside Pensacola; they toured Mobile, Pensacola and Florida Town, with owners and ads discussed.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Why 'Purple Derby'; Green Room dances and New Year's Eve at the Battle House
segments.summary: They discuss the purple derby hats, the 'hang on and ride' slogan, cover charges and long New Year's engagements from clippings.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Radio broadcast and scrapbook ads: Sanders Beach, Red Cross, Pleasure Palace
segments.summary: From the scrapbook: an Elks Club dance in 1926, a one-time Pensacola radio spot, hotel luncheon jobs and the 1927 Sanders Beach opening.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Teaching music and the Milton High job he did not take
segments.summary: He thinks about why he refused a teaching post at Milton High and says he gave students a start from a method book.

segments.chapter: Purple Derby Orchestra on the Gulf Coast
segments.title: Later posters: pickup dances, Slidell and rock-and-roll era billing
segments.summary: The interviewer reads later flyers, including a Slidell club billing him as father of jazz, and Pass Christian dates.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: Playing concerts at Morrison's cafeteria while working in the repair department
segments.summary: He played twice-daily concerts at Morrison's and pit work at the Capitol Theater while holding a repair-department job; digression on Al Galador.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: Joining Buzzy Williams at the Slipper, October 1928
segments.summary: A union magazine puts him at Morrison's in May 1928 and with Buzzy Williams at the Slipper that October; Lizana calls it a nice little place.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: The two Morrison's cafeterias
segments.summary: He played both Morrison's, one in town and one on the highway.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: Union resolution against signing contracts and Shreveport job lost
segments.summary: Asked about a 1928 union resolution, he recalls a Shreveport contract that fell through because he refused to join the union.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: Fellow musicians who worked at Whirlines
segments.summary: They try to place Johnny Harmon, Florese, a blind man, and trombonist Eddie Benton among coworkers at Whirlines.

segments.chapter: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
segments.title: Dropping out of music around 1931-32 during the Depression
segments.summary: After Morrison's, the Slipper, the Nut Club and the Ladoo he left music to settle down, returning only with later bands.

segments.chapter: Return to music and closing
segments.title: Hambone Inn, 1952, and Eaton's Club flyers
segments.summary: A photo shows him on sax at the Hambone Inn in Mississippi with Dan Seals, plus flyers for Slidell and Eaton's Club.

segments.chapter: Return to music and closing
segments.title: Playing again with the Brunies boys in 1952
segments.summary: They played together again in 1952, weekly dances, and the interviewer mentions seeing them with Jules Gallo.

segments.chapter: Return to music and closing
segments.title: Thanks and winding down
segments.summary: Mutual thanks as the interview ends.

segments.chapter: Return to music and closing
segments.title: John Handy and Sylvester: Lizana helped a young man get started
segments.summary: The interviewer says John Handy told him about Lizana; Lizana does not recall him clearly but the younger Handy credited him with help.

segments.chapter: Return to music and closing
segments.title: Tape running out and closing remarks
segments.summary: It is nearly ten o'clock, and the interviewer thanks him for making history.
